ety.text: PIE word *úd The adjective is derived from Middle English outre, utter, uttre (“situated on the outside of, exterior”), from Old English ūtera (“exterior, outer”, literally “more out”), the comparative form of ūt (“out”). Piecewise doublet of outer. The noun is derived from the adjective.

PIE word *úd From Middle English outren, utteren (“to display for sale; to market; to sell; to say, speak; to put into words, express, tell; to make known, reveal”), partly: * from outre, utter (adjective, adverb) (see etymology 1 and etymology 3) + -en (suffix forming the infinitives of verbs); and * from Middle Dutch uteren (“to announce, make known”) (modern Dutch uiteren); or from Middle Low German üteren, ütern (“to demonstrate, show; to speak; to sell; etc.”) (modern Low German ütern), from Old Dutch or Old Saxon ūtan, probably from Proto-West Germanic *ūtanā (“from outside or without; o…

PIE word *úd From Middle English outre, utter (“away, out; further away or out; out in the open; outside, without; to a greater extent”), partly: * from outre, utter (adjective) (see etymology 1); and * from Old English ūtor, the comparative form of ūt (“out; outdoors, outside”, adverb).

senses.d: To the furthest or most extreme extent; absolute, complete, total, unconditional.
ex: utter bliss    utter darkness    utter ruin
Oh VVarvvicke, VVarvvicke, I foreſee vvith greefe / The vtter loſſe of all the Realme of France.
Two cups of utter silver wrought and rough with imagery / I give you, which my father took from wracked Arisbe's hold; […]

senses.d: Of decisions, replies, etc.: made in an unconditional or unqualified manner; decisive, definite.
Further out than another thing; being the exterior or outer part of something; outer, outward; also, extremely remote.
ex: at the utter extremities of
[A]n hidden moth / The inner garment frett, not th’vtter touch; […]

senses.d: Succeeding all others; final, last, ultimate.
ex: Our vtter houre is come alas, fell deſtinies death hath brought.

senses.d: The thing which is most utter (adjective sense) or extreme.
ex: I take my leave, readie to countervaile all your courtesies to the utter of my power.

senses.d: Sometimes preceded by forth, out, etc.: to produce (a cry, speech, or other sounds) with the voice.
ex: Don’t you utter another word!
VViſdome cryeth vvithout: ſhe vttereth her voyce in the ſtretes.

senses.d: To verbally express or report (a desire or emotion, an idea or thought, etc.).
ex: Theeſe woords, vplifting both his hands, he to Iuppiter vttred.
VVhom ſhe all careleſſe of his griefe conſtrayned / to vtter forth th' anguiſh of his hart: […]

senses.d: To express (oneself) in speech or writing.
ex: I had tried to write a poetical epitaph, but in vain: my feelings refused to utter themselves in rhyme.

senses.d: Of a thing: to produce (a noise or sound); to emit.
ex: Sally’s car uttered a hideous shriek when she applied the brakes.

senses.d: To disclose or reveal (something secret or unknown); to bring to light.
ex: He that vttereth my counſayle ones I wyll neuer truſte hym whyle I lyue: […]
[W]ith vvhat gravity and Majeſty of ſpeech his Tongue and Pen uttered Heavenly Myſteries; […]

senses.d: To disclose or reveal the identity or nature of (oneself or someone, or something).
ex: […] God […] hath voutſafed to vtter himſelfe vnto vs in his Scriptures: […]

senses.d: To display or show (itself or something).
ex: […] Iuno, the Princeſſe, / Theare the pate, in digging, of an horſe intractabil vttred.
Give me the liberty to know, to utter, and to argue freely according to conſcience, above all liberties.
"Don’t worry about me," he uttered with minimum lip movement.

senses.d: Of words, etc.: to be spoken.

ex: [Y]ᵉ same [the book] was well vtteryd by yᵉ printar, & well lyked of in yᵉ comon weale, […]

senses.d: Further apart, away, or out; outside, without.
ex: A strawe, sayde Bele, stande vtter, / For we haue egges and butter, / And of pygeons a payre.
Gyue this gentylman rome, syrs, stonde vtter!

senses.d: To an extreme extent; altogether, quite.
